slides.title: Project Delivery Overview
slides.narration: Good morning everyone, and thank you for joining. I am presenting the Ricoh Project Delivery Overview on behalf of the FPT delivery team. Over the next few minutes I will walk through six things: how the team is structured, the offshore resource plan for the rest of the year, how we plan, monitor and report, the delivery approach we run today and the one we are proposing, how we intend to manage capacity and backlog for CPE and DCD, and finally the roadmap. The goal is to align on a delivery operating model for Q4 2026. Please feel free to stop me with questions at any point.
slides.notes: Cover slide. Period: Q4 2026. Presenter: FPT Delivery Team. Sections: Team Structure, Resource Plan, Governance, Delivery Approach, Capacity & Backlog, Roadmap.

slides.title: Products Supported by the Team
slides.narration: Let me start with the engagement overview. The team supports five products. Two of them are in active development: CPE, the Content Parsing Engine, and DCD, the Dynamic Cloud Database. The other three are in maintenance: VPD, the Virtual Printer Driver; REDE, the Ricoh Electronic Data Exchange; and RSI, Ricoh Smart Integration, which is our Boomi work. The team size is ten people, and we run a shared delivery model. CPE, DCD, VPD and REDE all draw on a shared pool of nine members, while RSI and Boomi has one primary engineer. On the Ricoh side, Jared and Niloofar are the stakeholders for CPE and DCD, Teyu for VPD, Phuc Nguyen for REDE, and Teyu together with Yuwen for RSI and Boomi. The key point here is that the same pool supports both product development and maintenance, which is what gives us flexibility, and also what makes capacity management important.
slides.notes: 5 products. Development: CPE (Content Parsing Engine), DCD (Dynamic Cloud Database). Maintenance: VPD (Virtual Printer Driver), REDE (RICOH Electronic Data Exchange), RSI/Boomi (Ricoh Smart Integration). Team size 10, shared delivery model. Coverage: CPE, DCD, VPD, REDE = shared pool of 9 members; RSI/Boomi = one primary member. Stakeholders: CPE and DCD = Jared, Niloofar; VPD = Teyu; REDE = Phuc Nguyen; RSI/Boomi = Teyu, Yuwen.

slides.title: Offshore Resource Plan
slides.narration: Now the offshore resource plan, with actuals from January to September and the plan for October to December. In the first quarter we ran at seventeen resources. From April to June that came down to eleven. July was ten and a half, and from August we have been at ten. The plan for October, November and December is to hold at ten. So the executive insight is simple: seventeen, to eleven, to ten, and the team has been stable at ten since August, with the same level planned through the end of Q4. In terms of allocation for the quarter: CPE has Do Luong, Tham Bui, Thoan Vo and Hien Le, plus shared management and DevOps. DCD has Dong Huynh, Huy Le, and fifty percent of Thoa Phung, plus shared DevOps. REDE has the other fifty percent of Thoa Phung. RSI and Boomi has Tien Nguyen at one hundred percent. And Quyen Le and Huy Nguyen work across products. One caution when reading the chart: because several people are shared, the product totals should not be added up as separate headcounts.

slides.title: Planning, Monitoring, Reporting and Governance Rhythm
slides.narration: This slide covers how we plan, monitor and report, and the governance rhythm around it. For planning, the backlog and tickets live in Azure DevOps. We do weekly priority and work planning, three-week sprint planning for CPE and DCD, and continuous intake for the maintenance products. For monitoring, we hold an internal daily meeting, we review the ADO board and tickets, we have a weekly meeting with Ricoh, and we review blockers and priorities. For reporting, a weekly status report goes out by email on Monday Vietnam time, which is Sunday in the US, to Jared and Niloofar, covering what is done, what is in progress, blockers, and the plan for the next week. Putting that together as a rhythm: daily for internal progress and blockers; weekly for Ricoh status and priority alignment; every three weeks for the CPE and DCD backlog review and sprint planning; and after each sprint, a retrospective to capture lessons and improvement actions. The decision flow runs from Ricoh stakeholders, to the FPT project manager and solution architect, to the product members, and then to QA and DevOps.

Monitoring: internal daily meeting; ADO board and ticket review; weekly meeting with Ricoh; blocker and priority review. Reporting: weekly status report by email, Monday VN / Sunday US, recipients Jared and Niloofar; contents Done, WIP, blockers, next plan. Decision flow: Ricoh Stakeholders → FPT PM / Solution Architect → Product Members → QA / DevOps.

slides.title: Current Hybrid Working Model
slides.narration: Before proposing anything, let me describe how the current model behaves. The operating flow today starts with a CPE or DCD backlog item, or an ad-hoc request, in Azure DevOps. Ad-hoc requests typically arrive by email from an end user or a dealer. From there we clarify, estimate and assign; then develop or fix and run FPT testing; then release and close. CPE and DCD already run against a defined roadmap and backlog. The issue is that ad-hoc requests layer on top of that, and their volume varies from week to week. Planned backlog and ad-hoc requests compete for the same capacity, and we have not yet established a consistent story point or velocity baseline. So why change? Three reasons. First, to formalize planning predictability for CPE and DCD. Second, to make the consumption of ad-hoc requests and support visible. Third, to protect the planned backlog from unpredictable ad-hoc volume. To be fair to the current model: its strength is high responsiveness. Its limitation is that unpredictable ad-hoc volume can crowd out planned work.
slides.notes: Current flow: CPE/DCD backlog item or ad-hoc request in Azure DevOps (ad-hoc arrives via end-user or dealer email) → clarification, estimation and assignment → development/fix and FPT testing → release and closure. Behaviour: CPE/DCD run against a defined roadmap and backlog; ad-hoc requests layer on top with weekly varying volume; planned backlog and ad-hoc compete for the same capacity; no consistent Story Point or velocity baseline. Why change: formalize planning predictability for CPE/DCD; make ad-hoc/support consumption visible; protect planned backlog from unpredictable ad-hoc volume. Strength: high responsiveness. Limitation: ad-hoc volume can crowd out planned backlog work.

slides.title: Proposed Hybrid Delivery Model
slides.narration: Here is the proposed hybrid delivery model. It treats the two kinds of work differently. For CPE and DCD product development, we move to a three-week sprint. Work is estimated in story points, we build a prioritized sprint backlog, the team does development and FPT functional testing, and each sprint ends with a review and outcome measurement. So the flow is backlog, story point estimate, three-week sprint, review and release. For the maintenance products, VPD, REDE and RSI-Boomi, we keep a continuous ticket flow: continuous intake and clarification, prioritization based on impact and readiness, implementation or issue resolution, and we measure it by throughput and cycle time. That flow is intake, prioritize, implement or fix, close. One clarification on releases: completed work can be released earlier when that makes sense, while the three-week sprint cadence itself stays fixed.
slides.notes: CPE/DCD product development: three-week sprint; Story Point estimation; prioritized sprint backlog; development and FPT functional testing; sprint review and outcome measurement; flow Backlog → SP Estimate → 3-Week Sprint → Review/Release. VPD/REDE/RSI-Boomi maintenance and support: continuous ticket flow; continuous intake and clarification; priority based on impact and readiness; implementation or issue resolution; measured by throughput and cycle time; flow Intake → Prioritize → Implement/Fix → Close. Completed work may be released earlier where appropriate; the three-week sprint cadence remains fixed.

slides.title: Outcome-Based Capacity for CPE and DCD
slides.narration: This is the capacity management framework for CPE and DCD, starting from October 2026. The elements are: a fixed three-week sprint; story points as the estimation unit; scope limited to CPE and DCD; commitment expressed as completed outcomes; and, for now, no historical velocity, because we have not measured it yet. The capacity split is seventy percent for planned backlog and thirty percent reserved for hot support. Because we do not have a baseline, we calibrate progressively over the first sprints. In sprint one we start story point estimation and record both delivery and support. In sprint two we review the consistency of estimates and the actual support usage. In sprint three we calibrate the estimates and review whether seventy-thirty is the right split. From sprint four onward we use a rolling average for forecasting. And an important rule: if the thirty percent reserve is not consumed, we pull additional backlog tickets according to the priority Ricoh has confirmed. The sprint does not end early.
slides.notes: Model from October 2026; planning framework for CPE and DCD. Sprint length 3 weeks, fixed. Estimation unit: Story Point. Scope: CPE and DCD only. Commitment: completed outcomes. Historical velocity: not yet available. Split: 70% planned backlog / 30% hot support. Baseline establishment: Sprint 1 = start SP estimation and record delivery/support; Sprint 2 = review consistency and actual support usage; Sprint 3 = calibrate estimates and review 70/30; Sprint 4+ = use rolling average for forecasting. If the 30% reserve is not consumed, pull additional backlog tickets by Ricoh-confirmed priority; the sprint does not end early.

slides.title: Execution Flow
slides.narration: This slide shows the execution flow and who decides what. Ricoh owns business priority. The FPT project manager and solution architect own impact, sequencing and capacity. The delivery team owns the story point estimates and the dependencies. And sprint planning is where the final CPE and DCD content for the sprint is decided. The diagram shows tickets moving from the backlog through the sprint stages into production. Meanwhile, the maintenance products continue through the continuous ticket flow we discussed, outside the sprint.
slides.notes: Decision responsibilities: Ricoh = business priority; FPT PM / SA = impact, sequence, capacity; delivery team = Story Point estimates and dependencies; Sprint Planning = final CPE/DCD content. Execution image: backlog → sprint stages → production with ticket types (defect, improvement, feature). Maintenance products continue through continuous ticket flow.

slides.narration: The CPE and DCD roadmap itself is covered in a separate presentation, the CPE and DCD Product Roadmap, so I will not go into the detail here. The point for today is that the roadmap feeds the backlog that the sprint model we just discussed will execute against.

slides.title: Questions and Alignment
slides.narration: That brings us to questions and alignment. The four things I would like us to align on today are: the hybrid model, with sprints for CPE and DCD and continuous flow for maintenance; the seventy-thirty capacity split and how we calibrate it; the prioritization cadence, meaning weekly alignment and the three-week backlog review; and the Q4 resource plan at ten people. I am happy to take questions on any of these.
